guide.title: Bousquet Mountain: from a 1932 mink farm to Mill Town Capital's 2020 purchase
guide.intro: Bousquet Mountain "dates to 1932 after Clarence J. Bousquet's mink farm failed during the Great Depression, and he started a ski club there," per the Times Union. The same article reports that Bousquet "partnered with General Electric's Pittsfield Plant to outfit the mountain with floodlights installed on poles in 1936 to illuminate runs, introducing the concepts of night skiing," and that among the ski area's innovations was "a rope tow gripper that protects the arms and hands of skiers, which Bousquet marketed and sold 500,000 units"; the same article separately reports that Bousquet produced five U.S. Olympic competitors. Bousquet's own homepage, in text accompanying an Instagram post, describes the operation as "the 5th oldest continuously operating ski area in the entire US," with "94 years of great vibes."

sections.heading: Mill Town Capital, a 2020 sale and a rebuilt lodge
sections.body: The Times Union reported on May 29, 2020 that Bousquet was being sold: "The Mill Town community impact fund is buying the ski area from the Tamarack Ski Nominee Trust and owners Sherry and PJ Roberts," with the sale "scheduled to close on Friday," the same day the article was published, covering 155 acres across four parcels, including the summit of Yokun Ridge, multiple buildings, and operational equipment. Mill Town CEO Tim Burke said, "We plan to invest in the ski operation infrastructure and the lodge" -- describing plans rather than completed work at the time -- and the article reported that the new owners would collaborate with Jon and Jim Schaefer of Berkshire East and Catamount, with Bousquet joining the Berkshire Pass season-pass program. NewEnglandSkiIndustry.com reported on June 15, 2021 that, "after one year of ownership, Mill Town Capital is continuing its major investment in Bousquet this summer": the old lodge was completely torn down in April 2021, and its replacement, a roughly 15,800-square-foot lodge "designed to better handle skiing and non-skiing operations," was expected to be ready for the 2021-22 season, at a cost the article puts at $5 million, citing the Berkshire Eagle. iBerkshires reported on November 28, 2021 that the resort would open that winter around "the modern 15,000-square-foot lodge that greets visitors from Dan Fox Drive," designed by Allegrone Construction with a gathering space, expanded dining options, a full bar, and outdoor seating; the same article describes Bousquet as part of "an outdoor recreation trifecta" that also includes the former Berkshire West, run as Bousquet Sport, and the former Lakeside Christian Camp, run as The Camp at Bousquet, and reports that the Pittsfield Finance Committee had recommended a tax increment finance agreement for the $11.3 million ski area, with the project separately receiving $960,000 in Pittsfield Economic Development Funds to connect water and sewer lines to the property.

sections.heading: In Pittsfield
sections.body: The Colonial Theatre at 111 South Street was built in 1903 and, per Wikipedia's article on the theatre, underwent an extensive refurbishment that concluded in 2006 following a National Historic Treasure designation, reopening the venue to the public. The Berkshire Museum, per its own homepage, is located at 39 South Street; Wikipedia's infobox for the museum lists an established date of 1903. Hancock Shaker Village's own website lists its site location as 1843 West Housatonic St., Pittsfield; per Wikipedia, the historic commune "emerged in the towns of Hancock, Pittsfield, and Richmond in the 1780s," but the museum's present visitor entrance places it in Pittsfield. Arrowhead, the house where Herman Melville lived and wrote Moby-Dick, sits at 780 Holmes Road; per Wikipedia's article on the house, it was designated a National Historic Landmark on December 29, 1962, and added to the National Register of Historic Places on October 15, 1966. Springside Park, per Wikipedia's article on the park, is a recreational city park on Pittsfield's north side spanning 237.5 acres, the city's largest green space; former mayor Kelton Miller began purchasing land for the park in 1908, and he and his wife Eva donated 10 acres to the city in 1910, with the park's historic district, centered on the circa-1856 Springside House, added to the National Register of Historic Places on June 27, 2008.

faq.question: Who owns Bousquet Mountain?
faq.answer: Mill Town Capital, through a purchase from the Tamarack Ski Nominee Trust and owners Sherry and PJ Roberts scheduled to close on May 29, 2020, per the Times Union. Mill Town Capital rebuilt Bousquet's base lodge in 2021, per NewEnglandSkiIndustry.com and iBerkshires.

faq.question: How old is Bousquet Mountain?
faq.answer: Bousquet dates to 1932, when Clarence J. Bousquet's mink farm failed during the Great Depression and he started a ski club on the site, per the Times Union. Bousquet's own homepage describes it as "the 5th oldest continuously operating ski area in the entire US."

places.name: Colonial Theatre
places.summary: A 1903 Pittsfield theatre reopened in 2006 following a National Historic Treasure designation and extensive refurbishment.
places.history: The Colonial Theatre at 111 South Street in Pittsfield was built in 1903; per Wikipedia's article on the theatre, following a National Historic Treasure designation, it underwent an extensive refurbishment that concluded in 2006, reopening the venue to the public.

places.name: Berkshire Museum
places.summary: A Pittsfield museum established in 1903, per Wikipedia's infobox.
places.history: The Berkshire Museum's own website lists its location as 39 South Street, Pittsfield, MA 01201; Wikipedia's infobox for the museum lists an established date of 1903.

places.name: Hancock Shaker Village
places.summary: A former Shaker commune museum whose visitor entrance sits in Pittsfield, though the historic commune itself spanned Hancock, Pittsfield, and Richmond.
places.history: Hancock Shaker Village's own website lists its site location as 1843 West Housatonic St., with a separate mailing address of P.O. Box 927, Pittsfield, MA 01202. Per Wikipedia, the historic commune "emerged in the towns of Hancock, Pittsfield, and Richmond in the 1780s" and is described as "a former Shaker commune in Hancock and Pittsfield, Massachusetts" -- the historic commune straddled town lines, though the museum's present visitor entrance address places it in Pittsfield.

places.name: Arrowhead
places.summary: The Pittsfield house where Herman Melville lived and wrote Moby-Dick, a National Historic Landmark since 1962.
